title: Aristocrat Ranchettes Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Aristocrat Ranchettes wells have a 55 ft median depth, but records range to 1,160 ft. See yield, water levels and drilling costs.
h1: Aristocrat Ranchettes Well Information for Buyers
intro_html:
Aristocrat Ranchettes sits on the plains in Weld County, with a large record of permitted wells within 5 miles. The records show a sharp split in drilling conditions: the median well is only 55 feet deep, but the middle half runs from 30 to 520 feet and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,160 feet.

Most reported wells produce useful water, with a 12.0 gallons-per-minute median yield. That does not make every lot equally easy to develop. Well depth, aquifer, water quality, septic layout and the exact permit history still need to be checked before you buy or build.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Aristocrat Ranchettes?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth is 55 feet. The middle half of wells falls between 30 and 520 feet, which is an unusually wide spread for planning a drilling bid. About 63% of wells are under 100 feet, while 22% are 600 feet or deeper. The 90th-percentile depth is 820 feet, and the deepest record is 1,160 feet.

This pattern means the median is useful for orientation, not as a promise for your parcel. Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, local aquifer selection and the location of usable water can move the required depth substantially. A driller should review nearby well logs, not just quote from the townwide median. Permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, Laramie Fox Hills and Alluvial formations.

sections.heading: Expected well yield near Fort Lupton and Lochbuie
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 54% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Six percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

For a buyer, that is a generally workable production picture, but the yield records cover only 803 wells. A yield test is still important because a strong nearby result does not guarantee the same result on your lot. Confirm the permitted use, storage and any pumping limits. An exempt household-use well remains subject to Colorado rules, including the 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit.

sections.heading: What the water-level records show
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median depth of 37 feet, with the middle half between 10 and 288 feet below the surface. That range matters for pump setting, trench design and the cost of lifting water to the house.

The decade series does not show a simple, continuous decline. The median was 19 feet below the surface in the 1960s, 405 feet in the 1990s, 211 feet in the 2000s, 107 feet in the 2010s and 16 feet in the 2020s. Those swings likely reflect changing locations and measurement coverage as well as groundwater conditions; only 239 wells report a static water level. Treat the series as a reason to inspect nearby measurements, not as proof that the water table is steadily rising or falling.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers serving this area
sections.html:
Weld County has a long well record around Aristocrat Ranchettes. Permits issued by decade were 102 in the 1950s, 193 in the 1960s, 309 in the 1970s, 233 in the 1980s, 573 in the 1990s, 702 in the 2000s, 511 in the 2010s and 340 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2026.

Domestic and household wells make up 54% of the use mix. Monitoring accounts for 22%, stock for 11% and irrigation for 10%. The most active listed drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Glover's Drilling (Glover, Jonathan M.) and Roger Schocke Well Drlg. Inc. (Schocke, Roger). Verify current licensing, availability and scope before relying on an old permit or contractor name.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost in Aristocrat Ranchettes
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,800 to $3,800. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $8,800 to $15,800 at the median depth. A deep result can change the bid quickly, especially because 22% of recorded wells are 600 feet or deeper. Ask for a written estimate that identifies casing, grout, pump capacity, storage, electrical work, trench length, water testing and any difficult-access charges. The final price should be based on the selected lot and a contractor's site review.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a lot
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The depth records show both shallow wells and very deep wells, so a dry hole or an unexpectedly deep completion remains a real planning risk. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable, even when nearby permits look favorable. Confirm casing and grout standards, construction details and the tested production rate.

Water quality also deserves its own investigation. Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 1,597 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a particular well, but it is a strong reason to test existing water and plan a baseline test for a new well. Keep the well, septic system and replacement area separated as required by the applicable rules.

sections.heading: Buying or building between Hudson and Brighton
sections.html:
Before closing, pull the DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and compare them with nearby wells in Aristocrat Ranchettes, Fort Lupton, Lochbuie, Platteville, Hudson and Brighton. Look for reported depth, aquifer, static water level, yield, casing and use. The local data is broad enough that a nearby address is more informative than the town median alone.

If you are building, make the well and septic layout part of the early site plan. Confirm legal water use, access for a drilling rig, electrical routing, storage needs and the location of a replacement septic area before finalizing the house. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Have a Colorado water attorney or qualified well professional review that issue before you spend on construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Aristocrat Ranchettes?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Aristocrat Ranchettes is 55 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 520 feet, 63% are under 100 feet, and 22% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,160 feet, so a parcel-specific log review is more useful than relying on the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Aristocrat Ranchettes?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,800 to $3,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $8,800 to $15,800. A deeper-than-typical well can raise the total substantially.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Aristocrat Ranchettes?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 12.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 6% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. These figures come from 803 yield reports, not every permitted well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Aristocrat Ranchettes?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit map alone. Within about 10 miles, records include 1,597 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well before purchase and establish a baseline test for a new well, using the property's location and construction history.

faq.q: Do I need to check water rights before building in Aristocrat Ranchettes?
faq.a: Yes. Most nearby permits are domestic or household wells, but the legal use depends on the permit and basin rules. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 100% of the aquifer records, and an augmentation plan may be required for some uses in an over-appropriated basin. Review the permit with Colorado DWR or a water attorney before building.
